newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul's Kim seeks economic cooperation on APEC trip.
newsitem.headline: Seoul's Kim seeks economic cooperation on APEC trip.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam headed for Vietnam on Wednesday, the first leg of the a nine-day trip that will focus on economic cooperation and security on the Korean peninsula.
After the Vietnam visit, Kim will attend the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Manila, Philippines.
"I believe my trip to Southeast Asia will help expedite peace on the Korean peninsula and our economic growth," Kim said at the airport before taking off for Hanoi.
Kim is scheduled to visit Malaysia between November 26-28 on his way back from the APEC meeting.
In Hanoi and Kuala Lumpur, Kim will demonstrate South Korea's commitment to fostering economic cooperation.
"Talks between businessmen accompanying me on this trip and their counterparts in the region will provide an opportunity for us to materialise our efforts," he said.
Kim will be accompanied by 69 South Korean business executives, including Sunkyong Group Chairman Chey Jong-hyon, who is the head of the Federation of Korean Industries.
Trade between South Korea and Vietnam totalled $1.54 billion last year, a three-fold increase from 1992, making South Korea Vietnam's third-biggest trading partner.
South Korean firms rank third behind Taiwanese and Singaporean companies in the growing list of countries that have poured investment into Vietnam's booming economy.
Malaysia is South Korea's 11th largest trading partner, with trade amounting to $5.47 billion last year. Malaysia is also one of the leading overseas markets for South Korean construction companies.
Although economic issues will take centre stage at the APEC summit, Kim is expected to take the opportunity to discuss security issues.

North Korea said on Tuesday it would temporarily abandon a border liaison office set up in 1992. The move indicated further deterioration of relations that turned icy following the incursion into South Korea of a North Korean submarine in September.
South Korea urged Pyongyang to reconsider the move, even though Seoul has said it would freeze all contacts with the North until Pyongyang apologises for the submarine intrusion.
In Manila, Kim is scheduled to hold summit meetings with U.S. President Bill Clinton, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Chinese President Jiang Zemin and other heads of states.
"During the summit meetings, recent security issues on the Korean peninsula and concerns of both nations will be discussed in great detail," Kim said.
